questions.stem: Which two scenarios are violations of integrity in the CIA triad? (Choose two.)

options.text: An attacker changes the amount on a stored payment record
options.rationale: Correct: unauthorized change to data.

options.text: Malware edits log entries to hide its activity
options.rationale: Correct: the logs were tampered with.

options.text: A DDoS takes the company website offline
options.rationale: That is an availability violation.

options.text: An eavesdropper reads unencrypted emails
options.rationale: That is a confidentiality violation.

options.text: A stolen laptop's customer list is read by the thief
options.rationale: That is a confidentiality violation.

questions.explanation: In the CIA triad, integrity means no unauthorized change. Tampering breaks integrity, eavesdropping or disclosure breaks confidentiality, and outages break availability.
questions.discriminator_tested: Tampering = integrity; disclosure = confidentiality; outage = availability.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT an internal threat?

options.text: An attacker overseas scanning the company's public IP addresses
options.rationale: Correct choice: the attacker is outside and has no legitimate access, so this is an external threat.

options.text: An employee who emails a client list to a personal account
options.rationale: Internal: the employee has legitimate access.

options.text: A contractor who misuses their VPN access
options.rationale: Internal: contractors with access are insiders.

options.text: An administrator who accidentally opens a firewall rule too wide
options.rationale: Internal: accidental harm by someone with access still counts.

questions.explanation: Internal threats originate from people or systems inside the organization that already have legitimate access, whether they act maliciously or accidentally.
questions.discriminator_tested: Internal threats already have legitimate access.

questions.stem: A former employee, whose accounts were all disabled last year, tries to log in to the company VPN from home using old credentials. How should this threat be classified now?

options.text: An external threat: the person no longer has legitimate access and must get past the perimeter
options.rationale: Correct: access, not past employment, decides the label.

options.text: An internal threat, because the person used to work there
options.rationale: Past employment doesn't count; their accounts are disabled.

options.text: Not a threat, because the old credentials won't work
options.rationale: A failed attempt is still a threat to investigate.

options.text: An internal threat, because the person knows the network layout
options.rationale: Knowledge is not legitimate access.

questions.explanation: External threats originate outside the organization and must first get past the perimeter. Once access is revoked, a former employee is an outsider, even if they know the network.
questions.discriminator_tested: External threats lack legitimate access and must get past the perimeter.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a function of network access control (NAC)?

options.text: Inspecting web page content and blocking gambling sites
options.rationale: Correct choice: content filtering is the job of a proxy or web filter.

options.text: Deciding whether a device may join based on identity and policy
options.rationale: A NAC function: it is the connection-time gatekeeper.

options.text: Checking a device's posture before granting access
options.rationale: A NAC function: posture assessment.

options.text: Quarantining non-compliant devices
options.rationale: A NAC function: enforcing policy on failures.

questions.explanation: NAC decides whether a device or user may join the network based on identity and policy, and enforces that at connection time. Filtering web content is a proxy's job.
questions.discriminator_tested: NAC is the connection-time gatekeeper, not a content filter.

questions.stem: Which risk does posture assessment most directly reduce?

options.text: Unpatched or unprotected devices joining the network and spreading malware
options.rationale: Correct: it checks device health before or during access.

options.text: Weak encryption on the wireless network
options.rationale: Wireless encryption is set by WPA2 or WPA3, not by posture checks.

options.text: Channel interference on 2.4 GHz
options.rationale: Radio interference has nothing to do with device health.

options.text: Dictionary attacks against the Wi-Fi passphrase
options.rationale: That is addressed by strong passphrases or WPA3's SAE.

questions.explanation: Posture assessment checks a device's health and compliance (patches, antivirus, configuration). Non-compliant devices are denied, quarantined, or remediated before they can do harm.
questions.discriminator_tested: Posture assessment checks device health before or during access.

questions.stem: Which statement about a guest network is NOT true?

options.text: Guests usually get full access to internal file servers
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: guests are kept away from internal resources.

options.text: It is a separate network segment for visitors
options.rationale: True: that is its purpose.

options.text: Internet-only access is typical
options.rationale: True: visitors usually need only the internet.

options.text: It is isolated from internal resources
options.rationale: True: isolation is the point.

questions.explanation: A guest network is a separate, restricted segment for visitors. It is isolated from internal resources, and internet-only access is typical.
questions.discriminator_tested: A guest network is isolated from internal resources.

questions.stem: Which two statements about NAC agents are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: A persistent agent stays installed on the endpoint
options.rationale: Correct: it is permanent software.

options.text: A nonpersistent agent is removed after the assessment, which suits guests and BYOD devices
options.rationale: Correct: it is temporary.

options.text: A nonpersistent agent stays installed permanently
options.rationale: That describes a persistent agent.

options.text: A persistent agent is the best choice for a one-time visitor's laptop
options.rationale: A visitor's device shouldn't keep company software; a nonpersistent agent fits better.

options.text: Using an agent removes the need for a posture check
options.rationale: The agent is how the posture check is performed.

questions.explanation: Persistent agents are permanently installed on the endpoint. Nonpersistent agents are temporary and removed after the assessment, which suits guest and BYOD devices.
questions.discriminator_tested: Persistent = permanent; nonpersistent = temporary, for guests and BYOD.

questions.stem: Which statement about a honeypot is NOT true?

options.text: It sits inline and blocks attacks, like an IPS
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: a honeypot is a decoy, not an inline blocker.

options.text: It is a decoy system meant to lure attackers
options.rationale: True: this is its purpose.

options.text: It has no legitimate use, so any interaction with it is suspicious
options.rationale: True: this is what makes it useful for detection.

options.text: It can help defenders study attacker behavior
options.rationale: True: what attackers do there is valuable intelligence.

questions.explanation: A honeypot is a decoy that lures attackers so they can be detected and studied. Because it has no legitimate use, any interaction is suspicious. It does not block traffic.
questions.discriminator_tested: A honeypot detects and studies attackers; it doesn't block.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT an example of a WPAN?

options.text: A city-wide public wireless network
options.rationale: Correct choice: city scale is a WMAN.

options.text: A Bluetooth headset paired to a phone
options.rationale: A WPAN: one person's devices at very short range.

options.text: A smartwatch synced to a phone
options.rationale: A WPAN.

options.text: A wireless keyboard and mouse connected to a laptop over Bluetooth
options.rationale: A WPAN.

questions.explanation: A WPAN is a wireless personal area network with very short range, such as Bluetooth between one person's devices. A city-wide network is a WMAN.
questions.discriminator_tested: WPAN is one person's devices at very short range.

questions.stem: Which ordering of wireless network types runs from the smallest scale to the largest?

options.text: WPAN, WLAN, WMAN, WWAN
options.rationale: Correct: personal, local, metropolitan, wide area.

options.text: WLAN, WPAN, WMAN, WWAN
options.rationale: A WPAN (a few meters) is smaller than a WLAN.

options.text: WPAN, WMAN, WLAN, WWAN
options.rationale: A WMAN spans a city, so it is larger than a WLAN.

options.text: WWAN, WMAN, WLAN, WPAN
options.rationale: This runs from largest to smallest.

questions.explanation: Scale grows from WPAN (one person's devices) to WLAN (a building or campus) to WMAN (a city) to WWAN (carrier coverage over large regions).
questions.discriminator_tested: WLAN sits between WPAN and WMAN in scale.

questions.stem: Which statement about a WMAN is NOT true?

options.text: It is the largest type, provided by mobile carriers across whole countries
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: that describes a WWAN.

options.text: It spans a city or similarly large area
options.rationale: True: metropolitan scale.

options.text: It is larger than a WLAN
options.rationale: True: a city is bigger than a building or campus.

options.text: It is smaller than a WWAN
options.rationale: True: WWANs cover larger regions.

questions.explanation: A WMAN (wireless metropolitan area network) spans a city or large area, between a WLAN and a WWAN in scale. Country-wide carrier coverage is a WWAN.
questions.discriminator_tested: WMAN is city scale, between WLAN and WWAN.

questions.stem: Which two are characteristics of a WWAN? (Choose two.)

options.text: It is provided by a carrier, such as a cellular operator
options.rationale: Correct: WWANs are carrier-provided.

options.text: It covers large regions
options.rationale: Correct: it is the largest scale.

options.text: It is limited to a single building
options.rationale: That describes a WLAN.

options.text: It reaches only a few meters, like Bluetooth
options.rationale: That describes a WPAN.

options.text: Its devices connect directly with no infrastructure
options.rationale: That describes an ad hoc network.

questions.explanation: A WWAN is a wireless wide area network with cellular-style coverage over large regions. It is the largest scale and is carrier-provided.
questions.discriminator_tested: WWAN is the largest scale and carrier-provided.

questions.stem: Which statement about a wireless access point is NOT true?

options.text: It is the client-side adapter installed inside a laptop
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: that is a wireless network access card.

options.text: It connects wireless clients to the wired network
options.rationale: True: it is the bridge between wireless and wired.

options.text: It is an infrastructure-side device
options.rationale: True.

options.text: Together with its associated clients, it forms a BSS
options.rationale: True: one AP plus its clients is a basic service set.

questions.explanation: A wireless access point (WAP) is the infrastructure-side device that bridges wireless clients to the wired network. The client-side adapter is the wireless network access card.
questions.discriminator_tested: The WAP is infrastructure-side; the access card is client-side.

questions.stem: A desktop PC with no wireless hardware needs to join the office Wi-Fi. The office already has working access points. What does the PC need?

options.text: A wireless network access card
options.rationale: Correct: the client-side adapter is what the PC lacks.

options.text: Another wireless access point
options.rationale: The infrastructure side is already in place.

options.text: A directional antenna on the access point
options.rationale: The PC still has no radio to connect with.

options.text: A WWAN subscription
options.rationale: That is cellular service, not the office Wi-Fi.

questions.explanation: A wireless network access card is the client-side adapter that lets a device connect wirelessly. The access point is the infrastructure side, which the office already has.
questions.discriminator_tested: The access card is client-side hardware.

questions.stem: Which two statements about wireless antennae are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: Omnidirectional antennas radiate in all directions for wide coverage
options.rationale: Correct: good for covering an area around the access point.

options.text: Directional antennas focus the signal into a beam for longer reach
options.rationale: Correct: good for long, targeted links.

options.text: A directional antenna is the best choice for covering a round open-plan office from its center
options.rationale: Covering all around a central point calls for an omnidirectional antenna.

options.text: Omnidirectional antennas reach farther than directional antennas of similar power
options.rationale: Focusing the energy gives directional antennas the longer reach.

options.text: Antennas only receive signal; they never transmit
options.rationale: Antennas both radiate and receive signal.

questions.explanation: Wireless antennae radiate and receive signal. Omnidirectional antennas cover all directions with wider coverage; directional antennas focus a beam for longer reach.
questions.discriminator_tested: Omnidirectional = wide coverage; directional = focused, longer reach.

questions.stem: Which statement about an independent BSS (ad hoc network) is NOT true?

options.text: Clients communicate through an access point
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: an ad hoc network has no AP.

options.text: There is no access point
options.rationale: True: that is what makes it independent.

options.text: It is peer-to-peer
options.rationale: True.

options.text: Devices connect directly to each other
options.rationale: True.

questions.explanation: In an independent BSS (ad hoc network), devices connect directly to each other with no access point. Traffic through an AP is the infrastructure model.
questions.discriminator_tested: IBSS has no AP; it is peer-to-peer.

questions.stem: A small shop has one access point serving a few tablets. The owner adds a second access point in the back room with the same SSID, connected to the same wired network. How does the wireless design change?

options.text: It goes from a single basic service set to an extended service set
options.rationale: Correct: two BSSs linked by the wired network under one SSID form an ESS.

options.text: It goes from an extended service set to a single basic service set
options.rationale: This is reversed: adding an AP grows the design.

options.text: It goes from an independent BSS to a basic service set
options.rationale: The original design already had an AP, so it was not independent.

options.text: It goes from a WLAN to a WWAN
options.rationale: Two APs in one shop are still a WLAN.

questions.explanation: A basic service set is one AP and its clients. Linking two or more BSSs through a wired distribution system under one SSID creates an extended service set.
questions.discriminator_tested: BSS = single AP; two or more linked BSSs = ESS.

questions.stem: When the office access point is switched off for maintenance, the wireless laptops can no longer reach each other, even though they are in the same room. What does this show about the network?

options.text: It is an infrastructure BSS, where all client traffic flows through the access point
options.rationale: Correct: with the AP gone, there is no path between clients.

options.text: It is an independent BSS
options.rationale: In an ad hoc network, laptops talk directly and don't need an AP.

options.text: It is a WPAN
options.rationale: A WPAN links one person's devices, typically over Bluetooth.

options.text: The laptops' wireless cards have failed
options.rationale: The timing points to the AP outage, not the client hardware.

questions.explanation: In an infrastructure BSS, clients communicate through the access point, so losing the AP cuts them off from each other. In an ad hoc network, they would talk directly.
questions.discriminator_tested: Infrastructure BSS: traffic flows via the AP.

questions.stem: Which statement about an SSID is NOT true?

options.text: Hiding it encrypts the network's traffic
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: the SSID is a name, not a security control.

options.text: It is the name that identifies a wireless network
options.rationale: True: that is what the service set ID is.

options.text: Several access points can share one SSID in an ESS
options.rationale: True: that is how roaming works.

options.text: Clients use it to choose which network to join
options.rationale: True.

questions.explanation: The service set ID is the network's name. It is not a security control, so hiding it neither encrypts traffic nor really hides the network.
questions.discriminator_tested: The SSID is a name, not a security control.

questions.stem: Which statement about an extended service set is NOT true?

options.text: Each access point must use a different SSID
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: an ESS uses one SSID across its APs.

options.text: It links two or more basic service sets
options.rationale: True.

options.text: Its access points are connected by a wired distribution system
options.rationale: True.

options.text: It lets clients roam between access points
options.rationale: True: this is its main benefit.

questions.explanation: An extended service set is two or more BSSs linked by a wired distribution system under one SSID, which is what lets clients roam between APs.
questions.discriminator_tested: ESS = multiple BSSs under one SSID, enabling roaming.

questions.stem: Which statement about nonoverlapping channels in the US 2.4 GHz band is NOT true?

options.text: There are about two dozen nonoverlapping channels to choose from
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: there are only three.

options.text: The three nonoverlapping channels are 1, 6, and 11
options.rationale: True.

options.text: With so few channels, crowding is common
options.rationale: True: neighbors often share channels.

options.text: Access points on channels 1 and 2 will interfere with each other
options.rationale: True: adjacent channels overlap.

questions.explanation: The 2.4 GHz band has only three nonoverlapping channels in the US (1, 6, and 11), so crowding and overlap are common.
questions.discriminator_tested: 2.4 GHz has only three nonoverlapping channels.

questions.stem: A new office sits among many other businesses' Wi-Fi networks and wants to minimize channel crowding. All of its laptops support modern standards. Which choice fits best?

options.text: 802.11ac in the 5 GHz band, which has many more nonoverlapping channels
options.rationale: Correct: more channels means less crowding.

options.text: 802.11ac in the 2.4 GHz band
options.rationale: 802.11ac operates in 5 GHz only.

options.text: 2.4 GHz, with every access point on channel 6
options.rationale: That piles everything onto one crowded channel.

options.text: 802.11n in 2.4 GHz, to get the most channel choices
options.rationale: 2.4 GHz has only three nonoverlapping channels.

questions.explanation: 802.11ac operates in 5 GHz only, where many more nonoverlapping channels mean less crowding than in 2.4 GHz.
questions.discriminator_tested: 802.11ac: 5 GHz only, with more channels and less crowding.

questions.stem: Which statement about 802.11n is NOT true?

options.text: It works only in the 5 GHz band
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: 802.11n works in either band.

options.text: It can operate in the 2.4 GHz band
options.rationale: True.

options.text: It can operate in the 5 GHz band
options.rationale: True.

options.text: It is older than 802.11ac
options.rationale: True: 802.11ac followed it.

questions.explanation: 802.11n operates in either the 2.4 GHz or the 5 GHz band (dual-band), so it spans both. 802.11ac is the 5 GHz-only standard.
questions.discriminator_tested: 802.11n spans both bands.

questions.stem: Which statement about Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) is NOT accurate?

options.text: Its only real improvement is a higher top speed for a single client
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is inaccurate: its focus is efficiency and capacity with many clients.

options.text: It is designed for efficiency in dense environments
options.rationale: Accurate.

options.text: It uses OFDMA to serve multiple clients at once
options.rationale: Accurate.

options.text: It suits crowded venues such as stadiums and airports
options.rationale: Accurate: dense environments are its target.

questions.explanation: Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) focuses on efficiency in dense environments, using techniques such as OFDMA. Its gains are efficiency and capacity, not just raw speed.
questions.discriminator_tested: Wi-Fi 6 gains are efficiency and capacity, not just speed.

questions.stem: Users on 2.4 GHz in one area suffer frequent drops. The area has a row of microwave ovens, many Bluetooth devices, and neighboring access points on overlapping channels. Which two changes most directly reduce this interference? (Choose two.)

options.text: Move capable clients to the 5 GHz band
options.rationale: Correct: microwaves and Bluetooth operate in 2.4 GHz.

options.text: Put the local access point on a nonoverlapping channel (1, 6, or 11) not used by its neighbors
options.rationale: Correct: this removes the overlap with neighboring APs.

options.text: Hide the SSID
options.rationale: The network name has no effect on radio interference.

options.text: Switch from WPA3 to WPA2
options.rationale: The security protocol doesn't change interference.

options.text: Install a host-based firewall on each laptop
options.rationale: Firewalls filter traffic; they can't fix radio interference.

questions.explanation: Interference comes from overlapping channels and non-Wi-Fi sources such as microwaves and Bluetooth, and 2.4 GHz is the more exposed band. Moving to 5 GHz and using nonoverlapping channels address both causes.
questions.discriminator_tested: 2.4 GHz is more exposed to overlap and to non-Wi-Fi sources.

questions.stem: Which range and speed comparison between the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands is NOT true?

options.text: 5 GHz generally reaches farther and passes through walls better than 2.4 GHz
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: 2.4 GHz has the longer range and better penetration.

options.text: 2.4 GHz generally has longer range
options.rationale: True.

options.text: 5 GHz is generally faster
options.rationale: True.

options.text: 2.4 GHz penetrates obstacles better
options.rationale: True.

questions.explanation: The trade-off: 2.4 GHz has longer range and better penetration but is slower; 5 GHz is faster but has shorter range.
questions.discriminator_tested: 2.4 GHz = range; 5 GHz = speed.

questions.stem: A café's Wi-Fi requires each guest to log in through a web portal with a code from their receipt, but the wireless network itself has no encryption. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Guests are authenticated, but their traffic is not encrypted, so others nearby can read it
options.rationale: Correct: the login proves identity but doesn't protect the data.

options.text: The portal login also encrypts the traffic
options.rationale: Authentication and encryption are separate functions.

options.text: The traffic is encrypted, so the login adds nothing
options.rationale: The network has no encryption.

options.text: Because a login is required, eavesdropping is impossible
options.rationale: Anyone within range can capture unencrypted traffic.

questions.explanation: Authentication verifies who connects; encryption protects the data. They are separate, so an authenticated but unencrypted network still exposes its traffic.
questions.discriminator_tested: Authentication (identity) and encryption (confidentiality) are separate functions.

questions.stem: Which statement about WEP is NOT true?

options.text: A long enough key makes WEP safe to use today
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: WEP's design is broken whatever the key length.

options.text: It uses the RC4 cipher
options.rationale: True.

options.text: Its short initialization vector is a key weakness
options.rationale: True: IV reuse is what makes it crackable.

options.text: It was the original Wi-Fi security standard
options.rationale: True.

questions.explanation: WEP, the original wireless security, uses RC4 with a short initialization vector. It is broken and obsolete, and never acceptable.
questions.discriminator_tested: WEP is broken and never acceptable.

questions.stem: Which statement about WPA is NOT true?

options.text: Its standard encryption is AES-CCMP
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: WPA used TKIP; AES-CCMP came with WPA2.

options.text: It uses TKIP
options.rationale: True.

options.text: It was a stopgap replacement for WEP
options.rationale: True.

options.text: It was superseded by WPA2
options.rationale: True.

questions.explanation: WPA was an interim replacement for WEP. It used TKIP so it could run on legacy hardware, and WPA2 replaced it with AES-CCMP.
questions.discriminator_tested: WPA = TKIP stopgap; WPA2 = AES-CCMP.

questions.stem: A small business's access points offer WPA2 and WPA (TKIP). Its devices are a few years old, and none of them support WPA3. Which setting is best?

options.text: WPA2 with AES-CCMP
options.rationale: Correct: the strongest option all of the devices support.

options.text: WPA with TKIP
options.rationale: WPA was a stopgap and is weaker than WPA2.

options.text: WEP, for maximum compatibility
options.rationale: WEP is broken.

options.text: Mixed WPA/WPA2 mode with TKIP enabled
options.rationale: Keeping TKIP enabled weakens the network for no benefit, since every device supports WPA2.

questions.explanation: WPA2 uses AES-CCMP and long served as the standard. When WPA3 isn't available, WPA2 with AES is the right choice over WPA/TKIP or WEP.
questions.discriminator_tested: WPA2 uses AES-CCMP, replacing TKIP and RC4.

questions.stem: Which two statements correctly compare WPA2-Personal and WPA2 Enterprise? (Choose two.)

options.text: Personal mode uses one shared passphrase for everyone
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Enterprise mode authenticates each user with 802.1X against a RADIUS server
options.rationale: Correct: individual credentials per user.

options.text: Enterprise mode uses TKIP, while Personal mode uses AES
options.rationale: Both modes use AES-CCMP; they differ in authentication.

options.text: Personal mode requires a RADIUS server
options.rationale: RADIUS is used by Enterprise mode.

options.text: Enterprise mode uses one shared passphrase
options.rationale: That is Personal mode.

questions.explanation: WPA2 Enterprise adds 802.1X authentication against a RADIUS server, giving each user individual credentials. Personal mode shares one key among everyone.
questions.discriminator_tested: Enterprise = per-user credentials; Personal = shared passphrase.

questions.stem: Which statement about IEEE 802.11i is NOT true?

options.text: It is the Wi-Fi Alliance's marketing name for WPA3
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: 802.11i is an IEEE standard, and WPA2 is its certification.

options.text: It is an IEEE standard for wireless security
options.rationale: True.

options.text: WPA2 implements it
options.rationale: True.

options.text: It replaced WEP's weak approach with stronger security
options.rationale: True.

questions.explanation: 802.11i is the IEEE standard for wireless security, and WPA2 is the Wi-Fi Alliance certification that implements it.
questions.discriminator_tested: 802.11i is the standard; WPA2 is its certification.

questions.stem: A company is buying all-new access points and laptops this year and wants the current generation of wireless security. Which should it deploy?

options.text: WPA3
options.rationale: Correct: it is the current generation, with a stronger handshake than WPA2.

options.text: WPA2 with TKIP
options.rationale: TKIP is a legacy cipher, and WPA2 is the previous generation.

options.text: WPA
options.rationale: WPA was an old stopgap.

options.text: WEP
options.rationale: WEP is broken.

questions.explanation: WPA3 is the current generation. It replaces the PSK handshake and resists offline password guessing, and new equipment should use it.
questions.discriminator_tested: WPA3 is the current generation.

questions.stem: Which statement about WPA3-Personal is NOT true?

options.text: It requires a RADIUS server for authentication
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: RADIUS belongs to WPA3-Enterprise.

options.text: It uses a passphrase
options.rationale: True.

options.text: It uses SAE instead of the WPA2 PSK handshake
options.rationale: True.

options.text: It resists offline password-guessing attacks
options.rationale: True: this is SAE's main benefit.

questions.explanation: WPA3-Personal is passphrase-based and uses SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) instead of WPA2's PSK handshake. Per-user RADIUS authentication belongs to WPA3-Enterprise.
questions.discriminator_tested: WPA3-Personal uses SAE with a passphrase; RADIUS is Enterprise.

questions.stem: What most clearly separates WPA3-Enterprise from WPA3-Personal?

options.text: Per-user authentication through 802.1X and RADIUS, plus an optional 192-bit security mode
options.rationale: Correct: individual credentials and the high-security suite.

options.text: Enterprise uses SAE with one shared passphrase
options.rationale: SAE with a shared passphrase is WPA3-Personal.

options.text: Enterprise works only in the 2.4 GHz band
options.rationale: Security modes are not tied to a band.

options.text: Enterprise turns off encryption to improve speed
options.rationale: Enterprise mode strengthens security; it doesn't remove it.

questions.explanation: WPA3-Enterprise adds 802.1X/RADIUS per-user authentication and stronger cryptography, including an optional 192-bit mode for high-security use.
questions.discriminator_tested: WPA3-Enterprise = per-user authentication; optional 192-bit mode.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a function of a firewall?

options.text: Luring attackers into a fake system so they can be studied
options.rationale: Correct choice: that describes a honeypot.

options.text: Permitting or denying traffic based on rules
options.rationale: A firewall function.

options.text: Enforcing policy at a network boundary
options.rationale: A firewall function.

options.text: Blocking traffic that doesn't match an allow rule
options.rationale: A firewall function.

questions.explanation: A firewall permits or denies traffic between networks based on rules, enforcing policy at the boundary. Luring attackers to a decoy is what a honeypot does.
questions.discriminator_tested: A firewall enforces boundary policy; a honeypot is a decoy.

questions.stem: A router needs a simple, fast filter that allows or blocks packets purely by source and destination IP, port, and protocol, with no session tracking. Which fits?

options.text: A stateless packet-filtering firewall
options.rationale: Correct: it judges each packet on its own by IP, port, and protocol.

options.text: A stateful firewall
options.rationale: A stateful firewall tracks sessions, which the requirement doesn't call for.

options.text: A next-generation firewall
options.rationale: An NGFW adds application inspection, far beyond a simple filter.

options.text: A proxy server
options.rationale: A proxy works at the application level for clients.

questions.explanation: A stateless (packet-filtering) firewall judges each packet alone on IP, port, and protocol, with no memory of sessions.
questions.discriminator_tested: A stateless firewall has no session memory.

questions.stem: A firewall allows a user's outbound HTTPS request and automatically lets the server's replies back in. It drops an unsolicited inbound packet that only claims to be a reply. Which type of firewall behaves this way?

options.text: Stateful firewall
options.rationale: Correct: it checks incoming packets against sessions it is tracking.

options.text: Stateless packet filter
options.rationale: A stateless filter cannot tell a real reply from a fake one, because it keeps no session state.

options.text: IDS
options.rationale: An IDS alerts; it does not allow or drop packets.

options.text: Wireless access point
options.rationale: An access point connects wireless clients; it is not a firewall.

questions.explanation: A stateful firewall tracks connection state and allows return traffic only for established sessions, so a packet that matches no session is dropped.
questions.discriminator_tested: A stateful firewall remembers sessions.

questions.stem: Which capability is NOT typical of a next-generation firewall (NGFW)?

options.text: Broadcasting an SSID for wireless clients to join
options.rationale: Correct choice: that is what a wireless access point does.

options.text: Application awareness
options.rationale: Typical: an NGFW identifies applications.

options.text: Deep packet inspection
options.rationale: Typical.

options.text: An integrated IPS
options.rationale: Typical.

questions.explanation: A next-generation firewall adds application awareness, deep packet inspection, and an integrated IPS, so it sees applications, not just ports. Broadcasting an SSID is an access point's job.
questions.discriminator_tested: An NGFW sees applications, not just ports.

questions.stem: Employees' laptops are often used on hotel and café Wi-Fi, outside the company's network-based firewall. Which control protects each laptop there?

options.text: A host-based firewall on each laptop
options.rationale: Correct: it goes wherever the laptop goes.

options.text: A bigger network-based firewall at headquarters
options.rationale: It protects only traffic crossing the headquarters boundary.

options.text: An IDS at headquarters
options.rationale: It sees only headquarters traffic, and it doesn't block.

options.text: A guest network at headquarters
options.rationale: That segments visitors at headquarters; it does nothing for laptops elsewhere.

questions.explanation: A host-based firewall runs on one endpoint and protects that device anywhere. A network-based firewall protects only the segment behind its boundary.
questions.discriminator_tested: Host-based protects one device anywhere; network-based protects a segment.

questions.stem: Which statement about an IDS is NOT true?

options.text: It sits inline and blocks malicious packets automatically
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: that describes an IPS.

options.text: It typically monitors a passive copy of traffic
options.rationale: True.

options.text: It alerts on suspicious activity
options.rationale: True: detecting and alerting is its role.

options.text: It can use signature-based or anomaly-based detection
options.rationale: True.

questions.explanation: An IDS monitors traffic, typically a passive copy, and alerts on suspicious activity. It detects and alerts but does not block; inline blocking is the job of an IPS.
questions.discriminator_tested: An IDS detects and alerts; an IPS blocks inline.

questions.stem: A company wants malicious traffic stopped automatically as it enters the network, not just reported. Which device and placement fit?

options.text: An IPS placed inline
options.rationale: Correct: it sees traffic in the path and can drop it.

options.text: An IDS on a switch mirror port
options.rationale: A passive IDS can only alert.

options.text: A honeypot at the network edge
options.rationale: A honeypot detects attackers but doesn't stop traffic to real systems.

options.text: A proxy for outbound web requests
options.rationale: A proxy handles clients' outgoing web traffic, not inbound attacks.

questions.explanation: An IPS sits inline and blocks detected malicious traffic. Because of that inline placement, a failure of the IPS can disrupt traffic.
questions.discriminator_tested: An IPS acts on threats from an inline position.

questions.stem: A brand-new attack with no published signature hits the network. Sensor 1 raises an alert because a database server's traffic suddenly looks very different from normal. Sensor 2 stays silent. What best explains the difference?

options.text: Sensor 1 uses anomaly-based detection; sensor 2 uses signature-based detection
options.rationale: Correct: only a baseline comparison catches an attack with no known pattern.

options.text: Sensor 1 uses signature-based detection; sensor 2 uses anomaly-based detection
options.rationale: This is reversed; there was no signature to match.

options.text: Both sensors use signature-based detection
options.rationale: Then neither would detect an attack with no signature.

options.text: Sensor 1 is an IPS and sensor 2 is a honeypot
options.rationale: The difference is the detection method, not the device type.

questions.explanation: Signature-based detection matches known patterns, so it misses novel attacks. Anomaly-based detection flags deviation from a baseline, so it can catch them, at the cost of more false positives.
questions.discriminator_tested: Signature misses novel attacks; anomaly-based detection can catch them.

questions.stem: Which statement about a proxy server or web filter is NOT true?

options.text: It looks only at IP addresses and port numbers, like a stateless firewall
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: a proxy works at the application level.

options.text: It makes requests on behalf of its clients
options.rationale: True.

options.text: It can filter content, such as blocked categories of sites
options.rationale: True.

options.text: It works at the application level
options.rationale: True.

questions.explanation: A proxy server, or web filter, is an intermediary that makes requests for clients and can filter content. It works at the application level, unlike a stateless packet filter.
questions.discriminator_tested: A proxy works at the application level on behalf of clients.
